# Exercise 6.3 — The same questions in R, with DALEX {#sec-dalex}

**45 minutes · work individually**

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Wrap a fitted tidymodels workflow in a DALEX explainer, and check that the
  explainer sees the outcome you think it does.
- Obtain global importance, a partial dependence profile and a local Shapley
  explanation from the same object.
- Say what a partial dependence profile assumes, and name a variable in this
  dataset for which the assumption fails.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-importance and @sec-shap were Python. The methods are not Python's: DALEX
gives you permutation importance, Shapley attributions, partial dependence and
individual conditional expectation from one explainer object, wrapped around
any model that can predict. This chapter answers the same questions in R, on
the same data and the same control column, so you can see that the conclusions
belong to the methods and not to the language. It also adds the one family of
plot that Python's `shap` does not give you, and that is the one with the
sharpest assumption buried in it.

## One explainer, any model

DALEX works by wrapping the model in a uniform interface: the data, the true
outcome, and a function that turns rows into predictions. Everything else is
computed from that, which is why the same code works for a forest, a
regression or something written by someone else entirely.

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)
library(DALEX); library(DALEXtra); library(vip); library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)
dia <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")),
         noise    = round(rnorm(n()), 2))

split <- initial_split(dia, prop = 0.7, strata = diabetes)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

rf_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe(diabetes ~ ., data = train) |>
               step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())) |>
  add_model(rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 3, min_n = 10) |>
              set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity", seed = 123) |>
              set_mode("classification"))

rf_fit <- fit(rf_wf, data = train)

explainer <- explain_tidymodels(
  rf_fit,
  data  = select(test, -diabetes),
  y     = as.numeric(test$diabetes == "pos"),
  label = "random forest",
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Read the `y` argument twice
`diabetes` is a factor, and `as.numeric()` on a factor returns the *level
codes* — 1 and 2, not 0 and 1. Pass that to `explain_tidymodels()` and the
explainer believes every patient has an outcome of at least 1 while the model
predicts probabilities below 1, so every residual is positive and the mean
residual is about 1. Nothing errors. The importance plot still draws. Compare
with `as.numeric(test$diabetes == "pos")`, which gives the 0/1 the explainer
expects.

The diagnostic is free: print the explainer with `verbose = TRUE` and read the
residual line. If the mean residual is not near zero, the outcome is wrong.
:::

```{r}
# the free diagnostic: residuals should straddle zero
round(summary(explainer$residuals), 3)
```

## Task 1 — Global importance, and the control for the third time

`model_parts()` is permutation importance: it shuffles each variable `B` times
and records the loss. For a classification task the default loss is one minus
AUC, so a variable that matters has a *higher* dropout loss than the full
model.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
set.seed(123)
mp <- model_parts(explainer, B = 20)
plot(mp)
```

`_full_model_` marks the intact loss and `_baseline_` the loss of a model that
predicts the mean, so the distance between them is all the AUC the forest has.
Turn the losses into drops and run the control check.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

losses <- as.data.frame(______) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(loss = mean(dropout_loss), .groups = "drop")
full   <- losses$loss[losses$variable == "_full_model_"]
drops  <- setNames(losses$loss - ______, losses$variable)
drops  <- drops[!names(drops) %in% c("_baseline_", "_full_model_")]

round(sort(drops, decreasing = TRUE), 4)
check_noise_control(drops)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")

losses <- as.data.frame(mp) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(loss = mean(dropout_loss), .groups = "drop")
full   <- losses$loss[losses$variable == "_full_model_"]
drops  <- setNames(losses$loss - full, losses$variable)
drops  <- drops[!names(drops) %in% c("_baseline_", "_full_model_")]

round(sort(drops, decreasing = TRUE), 4)
check_noise_control(drops)
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The quantity you want is each variable's mean loss minus the loss of the intact
model, which is the row `model_parts()` labels `_full_model_`. The object to
summarise is the one you just plotted.
:::

The picture matches Python's to the extent that you should expect: glucose far
ahead, age second, everything else in an undifferentiated band, and the control
inside that band at a few per cent of glucose.

## Partial dependence — the average patient who does not exist

A partial dependence profile asks: if I set this variable to $v$ **for every
patient in the data**, leaving all their other values alone, what does the
model predict on average? Sweep $v$ across the observed range and you get a
curve.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
pdp_glucose  <- model_profile(explainer, variable = "glucose",  type = "partial")
pdp_pedigree <- model_profile(explainer, variable = "pedigree", type = "partial")
plot(pdp_glucose, pdp_pedigree)
```

Glucose moves the average prediction from about 0.19 to about 0.74 across its
range — a real and large effect. Pedigree moves it very little, and most of
what movement there is sits at the sparse right-hand end of the variable.

## Task 2 — One curve per patient

The average hides how much the patients differ. `geom = "profiles"` draws the
individual conditional expectation curves — one per patient — with the average
on top.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
plot(pdp_glucose, geom = ______) +
  ggtitle("Ceteris paribus profiles for glucose, with the average")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
plot(pdp_glucose, geom = "profiles") +
  ggtitle("Ceteris paribus profiles for glucose, with the average")
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The argument is `geom`, and the value is named in the sentence above the cell.
`?plot.model_profile` lists the alternatives.
:::

Describe the spread. Do all patients respond to glucose in the same way, and
would you be happy to quote the average curve to someone asking about one
patient?

## Local explanation — the same patient, a different algorithm

`predict_parts(type = "shap")` computes Shapley values by sampling orderings of
the variables, rather than exploiting the tree structure as `TreeExplainer`
does. It is slower and approximate, and it works for models that are not trees.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
patient <- test[1, setdiff(names(test), "diabetes")]
patient

cat("predicted:", round(predict(explainer, patient), 3),
    " actual:", as.character(test$diabetes[1]), "\n")

set.seed(123)
local_shap <- predict_parts(explainer, new_observation = patient,
                            type = "shap", B = 25)
plot(local_shap)
```

The bars are the same quantity as @sec-shap's force plot, drawn differently and
estimated by a different algorithm. The boxplots behind them are the spread
across the 25 sampled orderings — a feature the Python plot does not show you,
and a useful reminder that these contributions are estimates with uncertainty
unless your model is a tree ensemble.

## Task 3 — The forest's own importance, for comparison

`vip()` reads the impurity importance the `ranger` engine stored while fitting.
Plot it, and put it next to the permutation ranking from Task 1.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
imp <- vi(extract_fit_parsnip(______))
imp
check_noise_control(imp)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
source("checks/checks.R")
imp <- vi(extract_fit_parsnip(rf_fit))
imp
check_noise_control(imp)
vip(extract_fit_parsnip(rf_fit), num_features = 9) +
  labs(title = "Impurity importance, from the fitted ranger object")
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`vi()` needs the model itself, not the workflow that contains it.
`extract_fit_parsnip()` reaches inside a fitted workflow and hands you the
parsnip fit.
:::

Same disagreement as in Python, in the same direction: impurity puts the
control fifth of nine at around 30% of glucose, permutation puts it in the
noise band at a few per cent. Two measures, one model, one figure each, and
only the second one is about prediction.

## The result that should bother you

Ask for a partial dependence profile of `insulin`.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
# the profile averages the model over the explainer's data, which is the test set
cat("rows with insulin recorded as 0:",
    sum(test$insulin == 0), "of", nrow(test), "\n")
cat("largest observed insulin:", max(test$insulin), "\n")

plot(model_profile(explainer, variable = "insulin", type = "partial"))
```

It is a smooth, gently rising curve, and it is nonsense. Three steps.

1. More than half the rows the profile averages over record insulin as exactly
   zero, which is not a measurement — it is a missing value written as a
   number, the defect you met in @sec-missing-data. The curve's left-hand end
   is the model's behaviour on "not measured", plotted as though it were a
   concentration.
2. The curve's right-hand end sets insulin to its maximum **for every patient**,
   including the ones whose insulin was never measured and the ones for whom
   that combination of values is physiologically impossible. Partial dependence
   averages the model over rows that do not exist and could not exist.
3. So the curve is well defined as a property of the fitted function, and it is
   not an answer to "what happens if insulin rises". That question is causal,
   and nothing on this page can answer it.

The same objection applies, more weakly, to every other partial dependence plot
you will ever be shown. Variables are correlated; holding the others fixed
while moving one walks you off the data.

## Reflection

1. DALEX and `shap` gave the same patient's explanation by different
   algorithms. What would you conclude if they had disagreed substantially, and
   what would you check first?
2. The partial dependence plot for glucose looks like a dose–response curve.
   Write the sentence that distinguishes what it shows from what a
   dose–response curve shows.
3. You have now explained this forest in two languages with four methods. What
   is the single piece of evidence that would most change your willingness to
   put it in front of a clinician — and is it on any of these pages?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) For a tree ensemble, TreeExplainer is exact, so a large
disagreement means the sampling estimate has not converged — raise `B` — or
that the two models are not the same model. Check the predictions agree first:
if the predicted probabilities differ, the explanations should. (2) The PDP
shows how the fitted function responds when one input is moved; a dose–response
curve claims what happens to an outcome when an exposure is changed. The first
is a property of a model, the second a property of the world, and only an
experiment or a carefully identified observational design connects them. (3)
The honest answer is external validation on patients from a different source,
and no, it is nowhere on these pages. @sec-shift is where that idea lives.

**Expected values.** Test AUC 0.75–0.80 — the explainer's `_full_model_` loss
is one minus that, so about 0.21. Permutation drops: glucose 0.14–0.18,
everything else below 0.025, `noise` 0.003–0.01 and 2–6% of glucose. Impurity:
`noise` fifth of nine at 28–34% of glucose. Patient 1 of the test set is
predicted 0.62–0.69 and is a true positive. Glucose PDP spans roughly 0.19 to
0.74; insulin PDP spans about 0.32 to 0.45.

**Common failures.** (1) `ranger` not installed — `rand_forest()` fails at
`fit()` with an engine error, not at `set_engine()`, which confuses people.
(2) Passing the workflow to `vi()`. (3) `as.numeric()` on the factor outcome:
worth setting deliberately as a five-minute exercise if the room is quick, as
it produces a plausible plot from a wrong explainer. (4) Expecting
`model_parts()` to be deterministic — it is not without `set.seed()`.

**Timing.** The chapter runs in under a minute but reads long. If you are
behind, keep the explainer, Task 1 and the insulin profile, and demonstrate the
rest. `modelStudio::modelStudio(explainer)` builds an interactive dashboard of
all of it in one call and is a good thing to show on the projector if the
package is installed; it is not in the booklet's dependencies.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Explain a model DALEX has never heard of
Fit a logistic regression with `glm()` and build an explainer for it with
`DALEX::explain()`, passing your own `predict_function`. Put its `model_parts()`
next to the forest's. The point is not the comparison; it is that the explainer
needed nothing from the model except the ability to predict.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Accumulated local effects
Re-draw the insulin profile with `type = "accumulated"`. ALE profiles average
the model's local slope over the data that actually exists, rather than over a
grid of invented rows. How much does the curve change, and does the change
support or undermine the reading you gave in step 3 above?
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that this forest, explained in R by three methods, tells the same story
as the Python explanations of @sec-shap — glucose dominates, nothing else is
clearly separated from the control, and the model's own impurity importance
disagrees with all of it.

**Cannot:** that any of this is evidence about diabetes. Every figure on this
page is a description of a function that was fitted to 537 rows of one
synthetic file. What that function has to do with patients is a question none
of today's tools can be made to answer — which is where @sec-day6-consolidation
leaves you.
